visible_difference: This is a genuine change of the performed action and is now physically achievable. Today B's hand rides the card, releases it at about 1.01 s, and the card glides into the tool on its own. The hand floats in the air until about 1.79 s, with the forearm stretched 12 to 24 percent and three fingers snapping in one frame. Under plan 14 the fingertip stays on the card's contact point from first touch at about 0.40 s until the card is hidden behind the tool base at world about (611,893). Nothing moves without visible contact, there is no glide, no airborne hand and no stretch, and the fingers blend continuously. This removes the defect class in the retained evidence: a card moving with nothing visibly moving it (B1 in 462fc3c5), B's 'wave, not a push' (selection.json), and NB1 and NB2 (51e65a10). B stays clearly different from A, a desk-level physical push against A's wall-chart key-strike send, and A is gated off. I checked the reach myself against the current code. The resting wrist is at world (338.0,1227.4) and the shoulder at (403.6,2401.8), a distance of 1176.2 against a maximum arm length of 1176.5, so the arm is already straight at rest. The hook needs the wrist at (689.6,1078.4), a shoulder distance of 1354, so the shoulder must move about 178 world units, mostly forward and up the desk. The s3 push to the chart edge needs the wrist at (539.4,1170.2), a distance of 1239, so a move of about 63. Both are reachable with constant segment lengths once the shoulder translates continuously, and the plan requires the lean to always reach the contact point and never clamp. What the lean looks like on screen: the shoulder stays off frame (screen y about 2800 in the hook and about 3100 in s3), so no torso is visible. The visible change is the elbow and upper-arm sleeve sliding forward at the bottom of frame, with the elbow at screen about (616,1636) in the hook and (707,1802) in s3. Because the resting arm is already straight, a minimum-lean solve leaves the elbow locked straight for the whole push. That rigid sliding rod would not read as an articulated performance. For the builder and the code re-review: lean somewhat more than the minimum so the elbow flexes visibly, about 10 to 20 degrees, during the reach. Let the hand bend at the wrist to follow the forearm, which tilts about 12 degrees in the hook. Verify at every frame that the fingertip is exactly on the contact point. These are implementation risks for the next review, not objections to the mechanism.
